definition: Authenticate means to prove that something is genuine or real.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word authenticate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know authenticate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The dealer's “moon rock” had sold twice before anyone thought to authenticate it.
To eyeball a signature is the lightest check of all — a quick once-over that settles nothing, far milder than authenticate.
Inspecting goes further than eyeballing but still stops short of authenticate: you examine the thing carefully without proving what it is.

To confirm is to check that a fact holds — a reservation, a rumor, a date. Authenticate goes to identity itself: it names the testing that proves an object is genuinely what it claims to be. You confirm that something happened; you authenticate what a thing is.

To certify is to issue the official paperwork — a seal and a signature declaring that a standard is met. Authenticate is the testing that comes first and proves the object real; a lab authenticates the manuscript, and an office then certifies the finding.

The “trench watch” at the estate sale fooled every casual buyer until a horologist tried to authenticate it: the luminous paint was decades too new, and the case bore a stamp the maker never used.
What looked like 1916 had been assembled in a garage last spring.
Authenticate is the right verb because the question is genuineness itself — not whether the watch is good, but whether it is what it claims to be.
Confirm would only say a fact checked out, and certify would issue paperwork; authenticate names the testing that proves an object's identity.
Reach for authenticate when the question is whether an object is the real thing — a document, a recording, an artifact.
Keep it apart from substantiate, its neighbor in this unit: you authenticate a thing, you substantiate a claim.

The jersey arrived at the county museum in a garbage bag, with a note claiming it was the one worn in the 1974 championship game — and no paperwork at all.
The curator wanted it to be real.
She also knew wanting proved nothing, so she sent the jersey to a textile lab to authenticate it properly.
The lab compared the stitching to game photographs, tested the dye against samples from the era, and ran the manufacturer's tag back to a plant that closed in 1976.
The jersey was exactly what the note said it was.
It hangs in the lobby now, above a small placard listing the tests — because, the curator says, an object is only as real as the checking behind it.
